cues.text: When money ran out
Romelu Lukaku was born in 1993 in Antwerp, Belgium.
His parents came from Zaire, which is now called the DR Congo.
His father, Roger, had been a professional footballer, and played for Zaire’s national team.
But from 1999, his father only played as an amateur, and money got very tight.
The family, in Wintam, had to sell things and be careful with food.
Sometimes they could not even pay for the electricity.
Switch the lamp back on.
When money is tight, it is never a child’s fault. Families can get through hard times together.
A promise to his mother
In those hard days, Romelu decided that he would become a professional footballer, like his father.
He had started playing at a local club, Rupel Boom, when he was very small.
Fold the promise into a heart.
He made a promise to his mother: he would be a professional player by the age of sixteen.
At Lierse he scored 121 goals in 68 matches, and at thirteen he moved to the big club Anderlecht.
A dream can give you hope on hard days. Make a plan, and take one small step at a time.
Asking for a chance
At fifteen, Romelu wanted more time on the pitch in Anderlecht’s youth team.
So he made a deal with his coach.
If he got more playing time, he would score at least 25 goals by December 2008.
That was a very bold deal to make.
Count the goals up to 25.
Romelu worked hard, and he reached 25 goals in November, a month early.
He had asked for a chance, and then he showed what he could do with it.
It is okay to ask for a chance. Then give it your very best.
A promise kept
On 13 May 2009, his sixteenth birthday, Romelu signed his first professional contract with Anderlecht.
He had kept the promise that he made to his mother.
Open the stadium doors.
Just eleven days later, he played his first match for Anderlecht’s first team.
The next season, he was the top goalscorer in the Belgian league, and Anderlecht became the champions.
In December 2009, he was voted Belgium’s biggest young sports talent of the year.
Keeping a promise takes time and hard work. Be proud of every step along the way.
Left on the bench
In 2011, Romelu joined Chelsea in England, a club he had loved as a boy.
But he hardly got to play, and spent most of his first season with the reserves.
When Chelsea won the Champions League in 2012, he would not hold the trophy.
He said it was not him, but his team that won.
Swing the sign to a new club.
Chelsea loaned him to West Bromwich Albion.
There, he scored 17 goals, more than any Chelsea player that season.
Being left out hurts. Keep working, and your chance can come somewhere new.
Speaking up
In 2019, Romelu moved to Inter Milan in Italy.
In his first season, some fans shouted racist insults at him.
Racism means treating someone unfairly because of the colour of their skin.
Romelu spoke out, and asked football to do more against it.
Raise the banner.
In 2020, after scoring, he knelt and raised a fist to support Black Lives Matter.
By then, the boy from Wintam was Belgium’s all-time top goalscorer.
Racism is never okay. If you see it or feel it, speak up, and tell a grown-up you trust.
